name: robots.txt (RFC 9309) + Cloudflare's Content Signals Policy (Sept/Oct 2025) + ai.txt (draft-car-ai-txt-wellknown-00, and the informal ai.txt/llms.txt convention) + IETF AIPREF working group (draft-ietf-aipref-vocab, draft-ietf-aipref-attach, Standards Track, updates RFC 9309) -- the machine-readable AI-usage-preference signal family, evaluated together with the HasData AI Crawler Block Index's live enforcement-measurement study (Tranco top 10k + Ben Welsh's 1,148-publisher news-homepages dataset, dated 2026-07-09).
kind: A layered stack of THREE distinct artifact types: robots.txt is a long-standing IETF standard (RFC 9309, 2022) being EXTENDED; Content Signals is a single vendor's (Cloudflare) proposed convention layered onto robots.txt syntax; ai.txt/llms.txt are informal, competing, non-standardized conventions; IETF AIPREF is the formal standards-track effort (two drafts: -vocab for the taxonomy, -attach for the attachment mechanisms) attempting to unify and formalize the space. Plus one independent empirical measurement study (HasData) of real-world adoption and, critically, ENFORCEMENT.
maturity: Mixed and important to this project's own governance_signal_handling field: robots.txt/RFC 9309 is mature and universally implemented. Content Signals is a live, large-scale vendor deployment (Cloudflare auto-enabled it for 3.8 million+ domains via its managed robots.txt feature) but not an IETF standard. ai.txt (draft-car-ai-txt-wellknown-00) is an early individual IETF draft, and llms.txt is a purely informal community convention with NO standards-track status and, per the measured evidence below, no crawler commitment to honor it at all. IETF AIPREF is standards-track (draft-ietf-aipref-attach-02 dated July 2025, expiring 22 January 2026, with a version -05 already superseding it per the fetch, indicating active iteration) and explicitly UPDATES RFC 9309 -- the most likely eventual converged standard, but not yet finalized.
license: Not applicable in the software sense -- these are protocol specifications and conventions, freely implementable; the HasData measurement study's own license/reuse terms were not confirmed.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extractor. The key distinction across the stack: robots.txt alone can only express a binary ALLOW/DISALLOW per path per user-agent -- it cannot distinguish 'you may crawl for search indexing but not for AI training,' a nuance ai.txt and Content Signals both exist specifically to add. Content Signals' own three-way split (search / ai-input / ai-train) KEEPS this nuance as a structured, machine-parseable line inside the EXISTING robots.txt file (no new well-known URI needed), while ai.txt/llms.txt DISCARD backward compatibility with existing robots.txt parsers by proposing an entirely separate file at a new well-known location -- a real adoption-friction tradeoff the evidence below shows playing out (Content Signals reaching millions of domains via automatic enablement; llms.txt stuck at single-digit percentages).
structure_preserved: IETF AIPREF's attachment mechanisms preserve preference structure at TWO levels: an HTTP `Content-Usage` response HEADER (applying to a specific representation/response, e.g. `Content-Usage: train-ai=n`) and a robots.txt-embedded `Content-Usage` RULE (path-scoped, using the same Allow/Disallow-style matching logic, e.g. `Content-Usage: /ai-ok/ train-ai=y`) -- giving both whole-site and per-path granularity. Notably, the -attach draft EXPLICITLY states it 'does not define any specific means of embedding preferences in content' (i.e. no in-document/in-DOM signal), acknowledging this as an open, format-specific problem the standard does not yet solve -- directly relevant to this project, since a per-element or per-fragment AI-usage preference (as opposed to per-page or per-site) has no standardized carrier at all yet.
interactive_elements: Not directly addressed by the signal vocabulary itself, though CAPTCHA and JavaScript-interstitial CHALLENGES are documented as a real-world ENFORCEMENT mechanism sites use IN ADDITION TO declared robots.txt signals (see measured_fidelity_cost) -- i.e. some sites pair a machine-readable preference with an interactive gate as backup enforcement, relevant to this project's gate_state_at_capture tracking.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not applicable -- outside the scope of any of these signal mechanisms.
layout_awareness: Not applicable -- all signal mechanisms operate at the HTTP/file level, never touching rendered layout.
javascript_required: Not required to READ any of these signals (robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt/llms.txt, and AIPREF's Content-Usage header are all fetched as plain HTTP resources), but IS relevant to ENFORCEMENT: the measured study found 5.0% of tested sites use 'Challenges/JavaScript interstitials' as an enforcement mechanism against declared-blocked crawlers -- meaning a JS-executing browser-based capture tool (like this project's own sensor) may be able to pass challenges a simple HTTP-fetch-based crawler cannot, raising a compliance question this project should treat carefully: technical capability to bypass a JS challenge does not change the underlying declared preference's meaning.
evaluation_method: The HasData AI Crawler Block Index used a genuinely rigorous LIVE measurement methodology: paired requests (one as GPTBot user-agent, one as a real Chrome browser) sent to the SAME domain from the SAME US-datacenter IP, on a 2,096-domain enforcement-testing subset (top 1,000 open-web domains + all publishers from the dataset), PLUS a 600-domain residential-IP sub-sample specifically to measure the datacenter-vs-residential enforcement gap -- a controlled, falsifiable, real-network methodology, not a self-reported survey.
corpus_size_and_origins: 10,894 deduplicated registrable domains total, combining the Tranco top-10,000 domain list (snapshot list 46XLX, dated 2026-07-09) with Ben Welsh's news-homepages dataset (1,148 publishers) -- giving both a broad open-web sample and a publisher-specific sample, a meaningfully large and dual-origin corpus by the standards of this whole research set. The enforcement-testing subset (2,096 domains) and residential-IP sub-sample (600 domains, with 250 specifically publisher domains in the crawler-specific pass-rate breakdown) are smaller but still substantial and methodologically justified subsets.
reported_precision_recall: Not a precision/recall study; its metrics are blocking-declaration rates and enforcement-compliance rates, both with clear denominators. DECLARED blocking (robots.txt Disallow/Content-Usage against GPTBot): 7.9% of the whole web (Tranco 10k), 50.5% of news publishers; ANY AI crawler blocked: 10.3% whole web, 56.4% publishers. Independent corroborating figures from other 2026 studies found in this research pass: 25% of top-1,000 sites block GPTBot (up from 5% in early 2023, per one study), 17.6% block GPTBot specifically (with only 6.6% blocking OAI-SearchBot, the citation-serving variant, showing sites discriminate between an AI crawler's TRAINING use and its SEARCH/CITATION use), 19.1% of a different tracked-sites sample block at least one AI crawler as of July 2026, and 9.9-15% ranges from yet other independently-run studies -- the SPREAD across studies (7.9% to 25% for GPTBot specifically) itself illustrates how sample composition (open web vs. news-heavy vs. top-N cutoff) swings the headline number substantially, a caution directly relevant to this project's own corpus_size_and_origins discipline. ENFORCEMENT compliance (the more important number): 39.5% of sites that DECLARE a GPTBot ban in robots.txt still served the crawler an HTTP 200 response when actually tested -- open-web sites ignored their own declared bans at 46.7%, publishers at 38.9% (i.e. publishers, who declare bans far more often, ALSO enforce them somewhat more reliably, but still fail to enforce over a third of the time). Adoption of the cooperative-signaling side: llms.txt adoption is only 7.9% whole-web, 3.2% publisher -- and STRIKINGLY, among the 56.4% of publishers who actively BLOCK AI crawlers, only 3.2% also publish llms.txt, an inverse relationship the study reads as evidence that blockers prioritize exclusion over cooperative signaling.
independent_oracle: The HasData study's paired-request, controlled-IP methodology IS itself a strong independent oracle for the ENFORCEMENT question (declared policy vs. actual server behavior) -- rather than trusting a site's robots.txt file at face value, it directly tests what the site's infrastructure ACTUALLY does when a real GPTBot-identified request arrives, which is a materially different and more rigorous form of evidence than most 'compliance' claims in this research space (compare to the WCXB/CleanEval-style items where the oracle is a single annotator's judgment, not an adversarial live test).
evidence_independence: The HasData study is an independent third-party measurement (not run by OpenAI, Cloudflare, or any site being measured), giving it strong evidence independence; Cloudflare's own Content Signals adoption figures (3.8 million domains) are self-reported by the vendor deploying the feature, so should be read as adoption-scale evidence (real) but not independently verified enforcement evidence.
page_archetype_coverage: The study's OPEN-WEB vs. PUBLISHER/NEWS split is a genuine, if coarse, archetype distinction, and the numbers diverge sharply by this split (7.9% vs. 50.5% GPTBot-blocking; 46.7% vs. 38.9% non-enforcement) -- directly validating this project's own page_archetype_coverage discipline: a single 'X% of the web blocks AI crawlers' number, without specifying which slice of the web, is exactly the kind of misleading aggregate WCXB's own methodology (item 1) warns against.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed -- no language/locale breakdown found in available sources for either the signal-vocabulary specs or the HasData measurement study.
leaks_outward: Not applicable in the runtime-telemetry sense -- these are declarative preference mechanisms, not capture tools; no outward leakage concept applies to the signals themselves.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable in the usual sense (there is nothing to hide -- these signals are DESIGNED to be discoverable), though the study's finding of '115 sites (5.5% of tested subset) blocked GPTBot despite robots.txt SILENCE, filtering at CDN/WAF layer without declared policy' is directly relevant: some sites enforce AI-crawler restrictions WITHOUT any discoverable machine-readable signal at all, meaning absence of a robots.txt directive is NOT reliable evidence that a site permits AI crawling -- a genuinely important negative finding for any tool (including this project's) that treats robots.txt silence as implicit permission.
countermeasures: The study catalogues real-world enforcement mechanisms in detail, useful as a taxonomy for what this project's OWN sensor might encounter when respecting a declared restriction: hard blocks (403/401/451, 22.2% of sites that declare a ban), HTTP 402 Payment Required (10.9% -- directly the subject of item 13), challenges/JS interstitials (5.0%), rate limiting/429 (2.4%), CAPTCHA (2.3%) -- with the REMAINDER (the 39.5% non-enforcement figure) simply serving content anyway despite the declared ban. CDN-specific enforcement posture varies enormously: Fastly 61.5% hard-block, Cloudflare 51.3% SERVE despite blocking policies existing at the platform level (16.9% hard-block, 24.7% challenge), CloudFront 78.5% permissive (largely unenforced), Akamai a mixed 39.1% serve / 34.5% hard-block / 19.5% rate-limit -- meaning the SAME declared robots.txt policy produces very different actual behavior depending on which CDN/WAF infrastructure sits in front of the origin, a fact this project should account for if it ever builds its own compliance-testing logic (checking robots.txt text alone is insufficient; actual server response to a real fetch is the ground truth).
measured_fidelity_cost: The residential-vs-datacenter-IP gap is the standout measured cost finding: against a residential-browser baseline pass rate of 77.2%, various AI crawler identities achieved markedly lower pass rates from a DATACENTER IP -- GPTBot 44.4% (33-point drop), ClaudeBot 36.8% (40-point drop), PerplexityBot 45.2% (32-point drop), CCBot 37.6% (40-point drop), Meta-ExternalAgent 38.0% (39-point drop) -- demonstrating that IP-origin-based fingerprinting/blocking is a SEPARATE, largely undeclared enforcement layer operating alongside (and often instead of) explicit robots.txt signals. IP rotation as a bypass strategy was found to be LARGELY INEFFECTIVE: only an 11-of-310 (3.5%) escape rate for rotating residential IPs against datacenter-blocked domains, i.e. blocking decisions are NOT purely IP-reputation-based and largely persist even when the requesting IP class changes.
gate_state_at_capture: This entire item is essentially the machine-readable half of this project's own gate_state_at_capture field, and the HasData study's enforcement taxonomy (hard block / 402 / challenge / rate-limit / CAPTCHA / silent-serve-anyway) is a ready-made classification scheme this project could adopt directly for recording what kind of gate (if any) was actually encountered at capture time, DISTINCT from what the site's robots.txt merely CLAIMS -- the study's central lesson is that declared policy and actual gate state are TWO SEPARATE facts that must both be recorded, since they diverge in nearly 40% of declared-ban cases.
determinism: Not deterministic across time in a meaningful sense for this project's purposes: robots.txt content itself CAN change between requests (the AIPREF -attach draft explicitly notes 'crawlers can cache a robots.txt file for up to 24 hours,' implying policy can and does drift), and enforcement behavior (per-CDN, per-crawler-identity) is a live infrastructure decision that can change independent of any declared file content -- meaning a single robots.txt check at one point in time is not a durable compliance record.
determinism_across_versions: Directly relevant: IETF AIPREF is ACTIVELY iterating (draft -02 fetched here, already superseded by draft -05 per the fetch's own note, with an explicit expiration date of 22 January 2026 for the -02 version) -- this project should expect the vocabulary and attachment mechanism to continue changing and should not hard-code a single draft version's exact field names into any long-lived implementation without a plan to track the spec's evolution.
reproducibility: The HasData study's methodology (paired user-agent requests from controlled IPs) is straightforwardly reproducible by design, and the underlying declared-policy data (robots.txt files) is itself always re-fetchable and re-checkable at any later time -- though, per determinism above, a REPEATED run would not necessarily reproduce the SAME numbers, since both declared policy and enforcement infrastructure can change.
failure_modes: Extensively and concretely documented, arguably the most empirically rich item in this entire research set on the specific question of 'do machine-readable preference signals actually work': (1) DECLARED-BUT-UNENFORCED bans (39.5% overall, 'paper-only bans... declared policy unsupported by actual enforcement') -- the single most important failure mode, meaning ANY system (including a well-intentioned crawler) that treats robots.txt Disallow as evidence the SITE OPERATOR successfully prevents unwanted access is simply wrong nearly 40% of the time; (2) UNDECLARED-BUT-ENFORCED blocking (5.5% of sites, CDN/WAF-layer filtering with no robots.txt signal at all) -- the mirror-image failure, where ABSENCE of a signal is also not reliable evidence of permission; (3) llms.txt's near-total lack of crawler commitment -- explicitly stated: 'OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Perplexity all read robots.txt. None of them have committed to reading llms.txt,' meaning publishing an llms.txt file currently provides NO enforcement guarantee whatsoever from any major AI crawler operator, despite its growing informal popularity as a convention.
failure_visibility: This is exactly the kind of SILENT failure this project's own commitments refuse: a site operator who declares a robots.txt ban believes they have opted out, receives no error or notification when that ban is ignored by 39.5% of would-be-compliant crawlers, and has no visibility into the gap unless they run exactly the kind of live enforcement-testing methodology HasData did. This asymmetry (the DECLARER has no feedback loop on whether their declaration is honored) is a structural flaw in the entire declarative-signal ecosystem, not a bug in any one implementation.
scale_limits: Not a compute-scale question for this item, though the CACHING behavior (robots.txt cacheable up to 24 hours per the AIPREF draft) does mean any policy CHANGE has a bounded but nonzero propagation delay across compliant crawlers -- a real-world latency this project's own policy-honoring logic should account for (a freshly-changed robots.txt is not necessarily immediately reflected in an already-cached crawl session).
delta_cost_model: Not applicable -- no incremental-computation concept in any of these signal mechanisms; each fetch of robots.txt/Content-Usage is a flat, independent operation (modulo the 24-hour caching window noted above).
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable -- no DOM-element-identity concept in this signal family.
adversarial_exposure: Not directly an adversarial-content concern (these are cooperative signaling mechanisms, not attack vectors), though the 39.5% non-enforcement finding has an adjacent adversarial-framing implication: a malicious actor impersonating a WELL-BEHAVED crawler (spoofing a compliant user-agent string while ignoring the very robots.txt it claims to respect) is functionally indistinguishable, from the SITE's perspective, from a genuinely non-compliant but honestly-identified crawler -- both simply fetch content the site's declared policy says should be blocked, and the site's own OWN weak enforcement (not any technical sophistication on the requester's part) is what lets both through.
provenance_carrying: Directly relevant: recording, per capture, (a) what the site's declared robots.txt/Content-Usage/ai.txt policy said AT CAPTURE TIME and (b) what actual gate/enforcement behavior was observed (per the taxonomy under countermeasures) gives this project a genuinely defensible, two-part provenance record -- directly actionable and directly aligned with the EDPB guidelines' own requirement (item 11) to 'honor and log robots.txt, ai.txt, CAPTCHA, and authentication barriers,' now with a concrete, evidence-based reason (39.5% non-enforcement) why LOGGING THE DECLARED POLICY ALONE is insufficient and the ACTUAL observed behavior must also be recorded.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/reparse concept in this signal family.
representation_cost: Not applicable -- outside scope; robots.txt/Content-Usage/ai.txt files are all small, fixed-format text files with negligible representation cost regardless of which project consumes them.
what_could_be_adopted: Four concrete, directly implementable mechanisms: (1) IMPLEMENT AIPREF's Content-Usage READING (both the robots.txt-embedded rule form and the HTTP response-header form) as the PRIMARY declared-policy signal this project's sensor checks before capture, since it is the standards-track convergence point most major crawlers are likely to eventually support, rather than betting on the non-standardized, unsupported llms.txt convention; (2) ADOPT THE HASDATA STUDY'S TWO-PART RECORDING DISCIPLINE as a first-class capture-metadata pattern: record BOTH the declared policy (robots.txt/Content-Usage/ai.txt content at capture time) AND the actually-observed gate/enforcement behavior (per the hard-block/402/challenge/rate-limit/CAPTCHA/silent-serve taxonomy) as two SEPARATE fields, never conflating 'the site says X' with 'the site actually does X'; (3) TREAT ROBOTS.TXT SILENCE AS INCONCLUSIVE, NOT AS PERMISSION -- per the 5.5% silent-enforcement finding, absence of a declared restriction does not reliably mean a site welcomes automated access, and this project's own policy-honoring logic should not treat silence as an all-clear signal, only as 'no declared preference found'; (4) IMPLEMENT THE THREE-WAY SEARCH/AI-INPUT/AI-TRAIN DISTINCTION (from Content Signals/AIPREF vocabulary) rather than a binary allow/deny, since this project's own use case (a browser-based sensor, not necessarily an AI-training-data harvester) may map most naturally onto the 'ai-input' (real-time retrieval/agent-use) category rather than 'ai-train' (bulk training-corpus collection) -- a distinction worth making explicit in how this project represents its own crawling INTENT to sites that check these signals.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- these signals classify SITE-LEVEL or PATH-LEVEL usage intent, not page-internal regions; no region-naming heuristic is introduced. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- entirely orthogonal to rendered layout. o_delta: NOT APPLICABLE, WITH ONE CAVEAT -- checking robots.txt/Content-Usage per domain is a flat, low-cost, non-incremental operation, but the 24-hour caching window means a naive per-page re-check could either (a) redundantly re-fetch the same policy file needlessly often, violating the SPIRIT of efficient incremental operation, or (b) cache stale policy past a legitimate site-operator change; a well-designed implementation should cache per-domain policy with an explicit TTL rather than either extreme. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AND STRONGLY REINFORCED -- the HasData study's entire value comes from testing REAL server behavior rather than trusting declared text, exactly the no-mocks discipline this project already commits to; adopting a 'verify actual response, don't just parse the declared file' testing posture for the project's own compliance-checking logic would be directly no-mocks-aligned. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- orthogonal to shadow-DOM capture policy, though both reflect the same underlying philosophy (honor stated/structural boundaries rather than covertly defeating them, and report honestly on what boundary was actually encountered). OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is and highly actionable -- this is the second item in this batch (after EDPB, item 11) where the recommended practice requires no technical reinterpretation, only a decision to implement the two-part declared-vs-observed recording discipline this research pass's own empirical evidence (39.5% non-enforcement, 5.5% silent enforcement) makes clearly necessary rather than optional.
governance_signal_handling: This field and this item are near-identical in scope; see gate_state_at_capture, provenance_carrying, and what_could_be_adopted above for the substantive content. The one remaining open design question for this project: whether to treat Content-Usage (AIPREF, standards-track, robots.txt-embedded) or ai.txt/llms.txt (informal, unenforced by any major crawler per the direct quote found) as authoritative when both are present and CONFLICT on the same site -- the evidence strongly favors weighting AIPREF/Content-Usage far more heavily given llms.txt's confirmed zero-adoption by major crawler operators.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not directly addressed by the technical signal mechanisms themselves, though directly complementary to item 11 (EDPB guidelines): the EDPB explicitly treats robots.txt/ai.txt as relevant to the GDPR 'reasonable expectations' balancing-test factor, meaning this project's adoption of the recording discipline described above serves BOTH a technical-governance purpose and a legal-compliance purpose simultaneously.
uncertain: Exact current version and content of the IETF AIPREF vocabulary draft (draft-ietf-aipref-vocab) was not directly fetched -- only referenced by the -attach draft; the -attach draft itself was confirmed at version -02 (July 2025) with a note that -05 already supersedes it, so exact CURRENT vocabulary terms beyond 'train-ai' were not independently confirmed

The HasData study's exact publication date/authorship and whether it has been independently replicated by a second research group were not confirmed -- treated as a single (if methodologically strong) measurement rather than a consensus finding

Per-crawler (ClaudeBot, CCBot, Google-Extended specifically) whole-web blocking percentages were not separately quantified in the fetched HasData content beyond the aggregate 'any AI crawler' figures and the publisher-specific residential-IP pass-rate breakdown

Whether Content Signals' three-way (search/ai-input/ai-train) vocabulary is fully interoperable with or converging toward IETF AIPREF's own vocabulary, or represents a genuinely separate/competing scheme, was not fully confirmed from available sources -- both exist and both were found actively referenced, but their long-term convergence path is unclear

The spread across independently-run 2026 studies of GPTBot-blocking rates (7.9% to 25%) was not fully reconciled -- likely explained by differing sample composition (open-web vs. news-heavy, differing top-N cutoffs, differing snapshot dates within 2026) but this was not independently verified
